citation.title: Exact Bias Correction for Linear Adjustment of Randomized Controlled Trials

standing_assumptions:
Setting, notation and standing assumptions, as printed. Every passage was read from the rendered page images (staged/pages/p-NN.png, and 220 dpi renderings of the same PDF pages for subscripts and primes). Pages are those of Econometrica, Vol. 92, No. 5 (September, 2024), 1503–1519, with the PDF page in parentheses (PDF p. 1 is the journal's cover sheet, so printed page = PDF page + 1501). Appendix A (pp. 1510–1512) and Appendix B (pp. 1512–1519) are inside the article; there is no supplement.
[Setting: Section 2, p. 1504 (PDF p. 3)] “We follow the setting of Freedman (2008a), Lin (2013), Abadie, Athey, Imbens, and Wooldridge (2020), and Lei and Ding (2021), which assume a Neyman model with covariates (Splawa-Neyman, Dabrowska, and Speed (1923)). There are $n$ subjects indexed by $i = 1, \ldots, n$. For each subject, we observe an outcome $Y_i$ and a column vector of covariates $x_i = (x_{i1}, x_{i2}, \ldots, x_{id})' \in \mathbb{R}^d$. Each subject has two potential outcomes $y_i(1)$ and $y_i(0)$. We observe $Y_i = y_i(1)$ if subject $i$ is assigned to the treatment arm $T$, and $Y_i = y_i(0)$ if subject $i$ is assigned to the control arm $C$. Let $D_i$ be a binary variable, where $D_i = 1$ indicates that subject $i$ is assigned to the treatment arm.”
[Design: p. 1505 (PDF p. 4)] “The experiment is assumed to be completely randomized, where $n_T$ out of $n$ subjects are randomly assigned to the treatment arm $T$ and the remaining $n_C = n - n_T$ subjects are assigned to the control arm $C$. Random assignment is the sole source of randomness in our statistical analysis. The potential outcomes and covariates are considered fixed, and the bias of an estimator is assessed relative to the randomization distribution of the estimator. We do not assume the existence of a superpopulation: the $n$ subjects are the population of interest.”
[Notation: p. 1505 (PDF p. 4)] “We define $[T]$ as the set of subjects chosen for the treatment arm, given by $\{i \mid D_i = 1\}$, and similarly $[C]$ as the set of subjects chosen for the control arm, given by $\{i \mid D_i = 0\}$. For a possibly matrix-valued variable $a_i$, we use the notation $\bar a = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n a_i$ to represent the population average, $\bar a_T = \frac{1}{n_T}\sum_{i\in[T]}a_i$ to denote the treatment group average, and $\bar a_C = \frac{1}{n_C}\sum_{i\in[C]}a_i$ to denote the control group average. The average treatment effect (ATE) can be expressed in this notation as $\mathrm{ATE} = \overline{y(1)} - \overline{y(0)}$, and the difference-in-means estimator is given by $\overline{Y}_T - \overline{Y}_C$. Similarly, we can write $\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_ix_i' = \overline{xx'}$ for $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and $\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i(1)x_i = \overline{y(1)x}$ for $y_i(1) \in \mathbb{R}$ and $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$.”
[Assumptions: p. 1505 (PDF p. 4)] “We make the following assumptions throughout the paper, which are standard in the literature.” ASSUMPTION 1: “For all $n$, there exists a finite constant $K$ such that $\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i(1)^2 \le K$, $\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i(0)^2 \le K$, $\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_{ik}^2 \le K$, for all $k = 1, \ldots, d$ and $d \le n$.” ASSUMPTION 2: “For all $n$ large enough, (1) $\bar x = 0$, and (2) $\overline{xx'} = I_d$, the $d \times d$ identity matrix.” ASSUMPTION 3: “Let $p_{T,n} = \frac{n_T}{n}$ and $p_{C,n} = \frac{n-n_T}{n}$ denote the inclusion probabilities into the treatment arm $T$ and control arm $C$, respectively. There exist positive constants $p_{\min}$ and $p_{\max}$ such that $0 < p_{\min} < p_{\max} < 1$ and $p_{\min} < p_{T,n} < p_{\max}$ for all $n$.” Then: “We shall hereafter omit the $n$ subscript in $p_{T,n}$ and $p_{C,n}$, and write $p_T$ and $p_C$ unless otherwise noted.”
[The two estimators: pp. 1505–1506 (PDF pp. 4–5)] “The first estimator results from a OLS regression: $Y_i \sim \alpha + \tau D_i + x_i'\beta$, (1) where one regresses observed outcome $Y_i$ on the treatment indicator $D_i$ and covariates $x_i$. We denote the OLS estimators for this case as $(\widehat\alpha, \widehat\tau, \widehat\beta)$. The estimator $\widehat\tau$ is hereafter referred to as the noninteracted ATE estimator. The second estimator results from an interacted OLS regression where researchers expand the covariates by including terms interacting the treatment indicator and covariates: $Y_i \sim \alpha_I + \tau_ID_i + x_i'\beta_{I,C} + D_ix_i'\beta_{I,T}$. (2) We denote the OLS estimators for the interacted case as $(\widehat\alpha_I, \widehat\tau_I, \widehat\beta_{I,C}, \widehat\beta_{I,T})$. The estimator $\widehat\tau_I$ is hereafter referred to as the interacted ATE estimator.”
[Section 3 objects: p. 1506 (PDF p. 5)] “As shown in Lin (2013), the noninteracted ATE estimator can be written as $\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}} = \overline{y(1)}_T - \overline{y(0)}_C - (\bar x_T'\widehat\beta - \bar x_C'\widehat\beta)$, (3) where $\widehat\beta$ is the OLS coefficient estimators for the covariates.” “The coefficient estimators $\widehat\beta$ can be algebraically written as $\widehat\beta = \widehat L^{-1}\widehat N$, where $\widehat L = I_d - p_T\bar x_T\bar x_T' - p_C\bar x_C\bar x_C'$ and $\widehat N = p_T(\overline{y(1)x}_T - \overline{y(1)}_T\bar x_T) + p_C(\overline{y(0)x}_C - \overline{y(0)}_C\bar x_C)$ by an application of the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem.” “The OLS coefficient estimators can be thought of as estimating the (finite) population coefficients $\beta^* = L^{-1}N$, where $L = I_d$ and $N = p_T\overline{y(1)x} + p_C\overline{y(0)x}$.” Footnote 4: “Note we shall hereafter assume for simplicity that all design matrices, $\widehat L$, are invertible. In the case of noninvertible design matrices, our debiased procedure will still work after choosing an arbitrary generalized inverse matrix and computing the ATE estimators accordingly.” “Let $y_i^*(1)$ and $y_i^*(0)$ be the centered potential outcomes, that is, $y_i^*(1) = y_i(1) - \overline{y(1)}$ and $y_i^*(0) = y_i(0) - \overline{y(0)}$. Denote the (rescaled) leverage of the $i$th subject as $h_i = \|x_i\|_2^2$. As in Lei and Ding (2021), we define the maximum leverage as $\kappa = \max_{i=1,\ldots,n}\frac{h_i}{n} = \max_{i=1,\ldots,n}\frac{\|x_i\|_2^2}{n}$. (4)”
[Section 4 objects: p. 1509 (PDF p. 8)] “We write the regression coefficient estimators of the pretreatment covariates in the interacted case as $\widehat\beta_{I,T} = \widehat L_T^{-1}\widehat N_T$ and $\widehat\beta_{I,C} = \widehat L_C^{-1}\widehat N_C$, and their (finite) population counterparts as $\beta_{I,T} = I_d^{-1}N_T$ and $\beta_{I,C} = I_d^{-1}N_C$, with $\widehat L_T = \overline{xx'}_T - \bar x_T\bar x_T'$, $\widehat N_T = \overline{y(1)x}_T - \overline{y(1)}_T\bar x_T$, $\widehat L_C = \overline{xx'}_C - \bar x_C\bar x_C'$, $\widehat N_C = \overline{y(0)x}_C - \overline{y(0)}_C\bar x_C$, $N_T = \overline{y(1)x}$, and $N_C = \overline{y(0)x}$. As shown in Lin (2013), the OLS regression-adjusted ATE estimator can be written as $\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}_I = \overline{y(1)}_T - \overline{y(0)}_C - (\bar x_T'\widehat\beta_{I,T} - \bar x_C'\widehat\beta_{I,C})$ for the interacted case, where $\widehat\beta_{I,T}$ and $\widehat\beta_{I,C}$ are the OLS coefficients on covariates $D_ix_i$ and $x_i$, repsectively.”
[Appendix A objects: p. 1510 (PDF p. 9)] “We define the following three constants: $N_{\mathrm{TTT}} = \frac{(n-n_T)(n-2n_T)}{(n-1)(n-2)n_T^2} = \frac{n_C(n_C-n_T)}{(n-1)(n-2)n_T^2}$, $N_{\mathrm{CCC}} = \frac{(n-n_C)(n-2n_C)}{(n-1)(n-2)n_C^2} = \frac{n_T(n_T-n_C)}{(n-1)(n-2)n_C^2}$, $N_{\mathrm{TTC}} = -\frac{(n-2n_T)}{(n-1)(n-2)n_T} = \frac{n_T-n_C}{(n-1)(n-2)n_T}$.” “Let $a = (a_1, \ldots, a_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $b = (b_1, \ldots, b_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$ be arbitrary $n$-vectors with fixed elements. We define the covariance estimator for the treated group as $\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_T(a,b) = \overline{ab}_T - \bar a_T\bar b_T$, and similarly for the control group as $\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_C(a,b) = \overline{ab}_C - \bar a_C\bar b_C$.”
[Readings fixed by the printed text and used in every target] (a) $\mathbf{E}$ (also printed $E$), $\mathrm{Var}$ and all probability statements refer to the randomization distribution: $[T]$ is uniformly distributed over the $\binom{n}{n_T}$ subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ of size $n_T$, $[C]$ is its complement, both arms are non-empty ($1 \le n_T \le n-1$), and everything else is fixed. (b) Vectors are column vectors and a prime is a transpose; for $n$-vectors $a$, $b$ of scalars, $\overline{ab}$ is the average of the products $a_ib_i$, so $\overline{hy(1)}_T - \bar h_T\overline{y(1)}_T = \widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_T(h, y(1))$, and $\overline{hy(1)} - \bar h\times\overline{y(1)}$ is the finite-population covariance of $h$ and $y(1)$ with divisor $n$. (c) $I_d^{-1}$ is printed for $I_d$ throughout, and the paper prints both $\hat N$ and $\widehat N$ (also $\hat N_T$, $\widehat N_T$) for the same objects. (d) In Assumption 1, $K$ is one constant, the same for every $n$: this is the reading the proofs use (the printed order of quantifiers is the clarity note P005-N002, not an error). (e) Assumption 2 is printed “for all $n$ large enough”; an exact finite-sample statement is read at a fixed $n$ at which (1) and (2) hold. Under Assumption 2, $\bar h = \frac1n\sum_i\|x_i\|_2^2 = \mathrm{tr}(\overline{xx'}) = d$, $h_i \le n$, and $\frac dn \le \kappa \le 1$ (the paper uses “$\kappa \in [\frac dn, 1]$” on p. 1516). (f) In Section 4, $\widehat\beta_{I,T}$ and $\widehat\beta_{I,C}$ are the within-arm slope vectors $\widehat L_T^{-1}\widehat N_T$ and $\widehat L_C^{-1}\widehat N_C$ defined there; their description as the coefficients on $D_ix_i$ and $x_i$ does not match parameterization (2), under which the coefficient on $D_ix_i$ is the difference of the two arm slopes (clarity note P005-E004, not an error). Every target uses the Section 4 definitions. (g) “Design matrices … are invertible” (footnote 4) is read as: $\widehat L$ (Section 3), respectively $\widehat L_T$ and $\widehat L_C$ (Section 4), is invertible under every assignment. (h) $O_p$, $o_p$, $O$, $o$ refer to a sequence of finite populations indexed by $n$, in which $d = d_n$, $n_T = n_{T,n}$, the covariates and the potential outcomes may all change with $n$; $\log$ is the natural logarithm.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Theorem 3.1, last part: the stochastic expansion of $\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}$ (noninteracted case)
canonical_claim.location: p. 1507 (PDF p. 6), Section 3; proof in Appendix B.1.1, pp. 1513–1515 (PDF pp. 12–14)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, p. 1507 (PDF p. 6)] Theorem 3.1 is stated “Under Assumptions 1–3” (its exact part is P005-T23) and ends: “If $\frac dn = o(1)$, we have the stochastic expansion $$\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}} = \mathrm{ATE} + \frac{1}{n_T}\sum_{i\in[T]}\big(y_i(1) - \overline{y(1)} - x_i'\beta^*\big) - \frac{1}{n_C}\sum_{i\in[C]}\big(y_i(0) - \overline{y(0)} - x_i'\beta^*\big) + O_p\Big(\sqrt{\frac{\kappa d}{n}}\Big).$$”
[The statement with the sequence made explicit] Consider a sequence of finite populations indexed by $n$ (dimension $d = d_n \le n$, covariates, potential outcomes and $n_T = n_{T,n}$ depending on $n$), under complete randomization at each $n$, satisfying Assumptions 1–3, with $\widehat L$ invertible (footnote 4). If $d_n/n \to 0$, then $$R_n := \widehat{\mathrm{ATE}} - \mathrm{ATE} - \frac{1}{n_T}\sum_{i\in[T]}\big(y_i(1) - \overline{y(1)} - x_i'\beta^*\big) + \frac{1}{n_C}\sum_{i\in[C]}\big(y_i(0) - \overline{y(0)} - x_i'\beta^*\big) = O_p\Big(\sqrt{\frac{\kappa_nd_n}{n}}\Big).$$
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
[Design and notation, p. 1505 (PDF p. 4)] “The experiment is assumed to be completely randomized, where $n_T$ out of $n$ subjects are randomly assigned to the treatment arm $T$ and the remaining $n_C = n - n_T$ subjects are assigned to the control arm $C$.” $[T] = \{i \mid D_i = 1\}$, $[C] = \{i \mid D_i = 0\}$; $\bar a = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n a_i$, $\bar a_T = \frac{1}{n_T}\sum_{i\in[T]}a_i$, $\bar a_C = \frac{1}{n_C}\sum_{i\in[C]}a_i$ for a possibly matrix-valued $a_i$; $\mathrm{ATE} = \overline{y(1)} - \overline{y(0)}$; $\overline{xx'} = \frac1n\sum_i x_ix_i'$, $\overline{y(1)x} = \frac1n\sum_i y_i(1)x_i$. $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathrm{Var}$ and probabilities are over the assignment, uniform on the $\binom{n}{n_T}$ subsets $[T]$ of size $n_T$; potential outcomes and covariates are fixed.
[Assumptions, p. 1505 (PDF p. 4)] Assumption 1: “For all $n$, there exists a finite constant $K$ such that $\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i(1)^2 \le K$, $\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i(0)^2 \le K$, $\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_{ik}^2 \le K$, for all $k = 1,\ldots,d$ and $d \le n$.” Assumption 2: “For all $n$ large enough, (1) $\bar x = 0$, and (2) $\overline{xx'} = I_d$, the $d\times d$ identity matrix.” Assumption 3: “Let $p_{T,n} = \frac{n_T}{n}$ and $p_{C,n} = \frac{n-n_T}{n}$ denote the inclusion probabilities into the treatment arm $T$ and control arm $C$, respectively. There exist positive constants $p_{\min}$ and $p_{\max}$ such that $0 < p_{\min} < p_{\max} < 1$ and $p_{\min} < p_{T,n} < p_{\max}$ for all $n$.” ($p_T$, $p_C$ are written without the subscript $n$.)
[Section 3, p. 1506 (PDF p. 5)] “$\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}} = \overline{y(1)}_T - \overline{y(0)}_C - (\bar x_T'\widehat\beta - \bar x_C'\widehat\beta)$, (3) where $\widehat\beta$ is the OLS coefficient estimators for the covariates” [of regression (1), $Y_i \sim \alpha + \tau D_i + x_i'\beta$]; “$\widehat\beta = \widehat L^{-1}\widehat N$, where $\widehat L = I_d - p_T\bar x_T\bar x_T' - p_C\bar x_C\bar x_C'$ and $\widehat N = p_T(\overline{y(1)x}_T - \overline{y(1)}_T\bar x_T) + p_C(\overline{y(0)x}_C - \overline{y(0)}_C\bar x_C)$ by an application of the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem”; “the (finite) population coefficients $\beta^* = L^{-1}N$, where $L = I_d$ and $N = p_T\overline{y(1)x} + p_C\overline{y(0)x}$”; “$y_i^*(1) = y_i(1) - \overline{y(1)}$ and $y_i^*(0) = y_i(0) - \overline{y(0)}$. Denote the (rescaled) leverage of the $i$th subject as $h_i = \|x_i\|_2^2$”; “$\kappa = \max_{i=1,\ldots,n}\frac{h_i}{n} = \max_{i=1,\ldots,n}\frac{\|x_i\|_2^2}{n}$. (4)” Footnote 4: “Note we shall hereafter assume for simplicity that all design matrices, $\widehat L$, are invertible. In the case of noninvertible design matrices, our debiased procedure will still work after choosing an arbitrary generalized inverse matrix and computing the ATE estimators accordingly.”
[Appendix B.1.1, p. 1513 (PDF p. 12)] “Let $(\alpha^*, \tau^*, \beta^*)$ be the minimizer of the criterion $p_T\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i(1) - \alpha - \tau - x_i'\beta)^2 + p_C\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i(0) - \alpha - x_i'\beta)^2$.” Equation (9) gives $(\alpha^*, \tau^*, \beta^*)' = O^{-1}\big(p_T\overline{y(1)} + p_C\overline{y(0)},\ p_T\overline{y(1)},\ (p_T\overline{y(1)x} + p_C\overline{y(0)x})'\big)'$ with $O$ the block matrix with rows $(1, p_T, 0_{1\times d})$, $(p_T, p_T, 0_{1\times d})$, $(0_{d\times1}, 0_{d\times1}, I_d)$; under Assumption 2 this is $\alpha^* = \overline{y(0)}$, $\tau^* = \overline{y(1)} - \overline{y(0)}$, $\beta^* = N$. “Define $e_i(1) = y_i(1) - \alpha^* - \tau^* - x_i'\beta^*$ and $e_i(0) = y_i(0) - \alpha^* - x_i'\beta^*$.” “We can represent the observed outcome as $Y_i = \alpha^* + \tau^*D_i + x_i'\beta^* + e_i(D_i)$.” Equation (10): $(\widehat\alpha, \widehat\tau, \widehat\beta')' - (\alpha^*, \tau^*, \beta^{*\prime})' = \widehat O^{-1}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(1, D_i, x_i')'e_i(D_i)$ with $\widehat O$ the block matrix with rows $(1, p_T, 0_{1\times d})$, $(p_T, p_T, p_T\bar x_T')$, $(0_{d\times1}, p_T\bar x_T, I_d)$. “Define $\tilde x_i = (1, D_i, x_i)'$ and $x_i^o = (0, 0, x_i)'$. We have the decomposition $(\bar x_T - \bar x_C)'(\widehat\beta - \beta^*) = \underbrace{(\bar x_T - \bar x_C)'\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_ie_i(D_i)}_{(*)} + \underbrace{(\bar x_T^o - \bar x_C^o)'\big(\widehat O^{-1} - O^{-1}\big)\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\tilde x_ie_i(D_i)}_{(**)}$.”
[Reading of the order symbols] A sequence of finite populations indexed by $n$: for each $n$, a dimension $d = d_n$ with $1 \le d_n \le n$, covariates $x_1,\ldots,x_n \in \mathbb{R}^{d_n}$, potential outcomes $y_i(1), y_i(0)$ and an arm size $n_T = n_{T,n}$, all of which may change with $n$; Assumption 1 holds with one constant $K$ for all $n$, Assumption 2 for all $n$ large enough, Assumption 3 with fixed $p_{\min}, p_{\max}$; the design matrices are invertible under every assignment (footnote 4). For random variables $R_n$ on the randomization spaces and positive numbers $r_n$: $R_n = O_p(r_n)$ means that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there are $M < \infty$ and $n_0$ with $\Pr(|R_n| > Mr_n) < \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge n_0$; $R_n = o_p(r_n)$ means that $\Pr(|R_n| > \delta r_n) \to 0$ for every $\delta > 0$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Exact statements for each fixed $n$ at which Assumption 2 holds, from the printed proof (B.1.1): (1) $R_n = -(\bar x_T - \bar x_C)'(\widehat\beta - \beta^*)$ (from (3) and $\beta^* = N$). (2) Equation (9) and its consequence $\alpha^* = \overline{y(0)}$, $\tau^* = \overline{y(1)} - \overline{y(0)}$, $\beta^* = N$; the normal equation $p_T\sum_ix_ie_i(1) + p_C\sum_ix_ie_i(0) = 0$; and $p_T\frac1n\sum_ie_i(1)^2 + p_C\frac1n\sum_ie_i(0)^2 \le p_T\frac1n\sum_iy_i(1)^2 + p_C\frac1n\sum_iy_i(0)^2$ (p. 1513). (3) The representation (10) and the decomposition $(\bar x_T - \bar x_C)'(\widehat\beta - \beta^*) = (*) + (**)$ (p. 1513). (4) $\bar x_T - \bar x_C = \frac{1}{p_C}\bar x_T$ and the three-line identity for $(*)$ (p. 1514; P005-T18). (5) $\mathbf{E}[(*)] = \frac{1}{p_Cnn_T}\frac{n_Tn_C}{n(n-1)}\sum_i\|x_i\|_2^2\big(e_i(1) - e_i(0)\big) = \frac{1}{n-1}\cdot\frac1n\sum_ih_i\big(e_i(1) - e_i(0)\big)$ (p. 1514), and $\big|\frac1n\sum_ih_i\delta_i\big| \le \sqrt{n\kappa d}\,\sqrt{\frac1n\sum_i\delta_i^2}$ with $\delta_i = e_i(1) - e_i(0)$ (Cauchy–Schwarz and $\frac1n\sum_ih_i^2 \le n\kappa d$). (6) The variance bound for $(*)$: for an $n \times n$ matrix $B$ with zero row and column sums and $n \ge 4$, $\mathrm{Var}\big(\sum_{i,j\in[T]}B_{ij}\big) \le \frac{n_Tn_C}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i,j}B_{ij}^2$ (the fact taken from Lemma A.5 of Lei and Ding (2021); proved in the N004 derivation, section 4), applied to $B_{ij} = x_i'(x_j\delta_j - \frac1n\sum_kx_k\delta_k)$; then the corrected chain of P005-T17, giving $\mathrm{Var}[(*)] \le \frac{\kappa}{p_Tp_C(n-1)}\cdot\frac1n\sum_j\delta_j^2$. (7) For $(**)$: $|||O - \widehat O|||_2 \le \|O - \widehat O\|_2 = \sqrt{2p_T^2\sum_{k=1}^d\big(\frac{1}{n_T}\sum_{i\in[T]}x_{ik}\big)^2} = \sqrt2\,p_T\|\bar x_T\|_2$ (operator norm bounded by the Frobenius norm, p. 1515), with $\mathbf{E}\|\bar x_T\|_2^2 = \frac{n_C}{n_T(n-1)}d$. The limit steps printed after these: $|||O^{-1} - \widehat O^{-1}|||_2 = O_p(\sqrt{d/n})$ if $d/n = o(1)$, the eigenvalues of $O$ being bounded above and below by Assumption 3, and “A simple calculation shows that the term $(**)$ is of the order $o_p(\sqrt{\frac{\kappa d}{n}})$”.
canonical_claim.note: One of the four expansions behind headline claim P005-H5 (the bias-corrected estimators have the same limiting distributions as the uncorrected ones). Opus followed B.1.1 line by line and found the remainder order correct ($\mathbf{E}[(*)] = \mathrm{mean}(h(e(1) - e(0)))/(n-1) = O(\sqrt{\kappa d/n})$, $\mathrm{Var}[(*)] = O(\kappa/n)$, $(**) = O_p((d/n)\sqrt\kappa)$); the proof contains the misprints P005-E007 (P005-T17) and P005-N005 (P005-T18), which do not change the rate. The quadratic-form mean and variance facts imported from Lei and Ding (2021) are derived independently in the validator's derivation for P005-N004, section 4 (the artifact named). The paper states no central limit theorem; equality of the limiting distributions of $\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}$ and $\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}_{\mathrm{Debiased}}$ follows from this expansion and P005-T26 when $\kappa d \to 0$, for example for fixed $d$ under Remark 4's moment condition; the readers note that for growing $d$ the condition $\kappa d \to 0$ is not stated (P005-N001 and P005-N003 were not confirmed as errors).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Theorem 3.2, second part: the asymptotic linear expansion of $\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}_{\mathrm{Debiased}}$
canonical_claim.location: p. 1509 (PDF p. 8), Section 3 (the theorem begins on p. 1508, PDF p. 7); proof in Appendix B.2, pp. 1516–1517 (PDF pp. 15–16)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, p. 1509 (PDF p. 8)] Theorem 3.2 (its first part is P005-T21) ends: “Under Assumptions 1–3 and if $\kappa = o(1)$, the estimator $\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}_{\mathrm{Debiased}}$ has the asymptotic linear expansion $$\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}_{\mathrm{Debiased}} = \mathrm{ATE} + \frac{1}{n_T}\sum_{i\in[T]}\big(y_i(1) - \overline{y(1)} - x_i'\beta^*\big) - \frac{1}{n_C}\sum_{i\in[C]}\big(y_i(0) - \overline{y(0)} - x_i'\beta^*\big) + o_p\Big(\sqrt{\frac1n}\Big).$$”
[The statement with the sequence made explicit] Consider a sequence of finite populations indexed by $n$ (dimension $d = d_n \le n$, covariates, potential outcomes and $n_T = n_{T,n}$ depending on $n$), under complete randomization at each $n$, satisfying Assumptions 1–3, with $\widehat L$ invertible (footnote 4). If $\kappa_n \to 0$, then $$\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}_{\mathrm{Debiased}} - \mathrm{ATE} - \frac{1}{n_T}\sum_{i\in[T]}\big(y_i(1) - \overline{y(1)} - x_i'\beta^*\big) + \frac{1}{n_C}\sum_{i\in[C]}\big(y_i(0) - \overline{y(0)} - x_i'\beta^*\big) = o_p\big(n^{-1/2}\big).$$ The printed proof shows more: without the condition $\kappa = o(1)$, the left-hand side is the term $(*)$ of p. 1516 and $(*) = O_p\big(\sqrt{\kappa/n}\big)$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:

[Printed, p. 1510 (PDF p. 9)] Theorem 4.2 (its first part is P005-T22) ends: “Under Assumptions 1–3 and $\kappa = o(1)$, the estimator $\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}_{I,\mathrm{Debiased}}$ has the asymptotic linear expansion $$\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}_{I,\mathrm{Debiased}} = \overline{y(1)} - \overline{y(0)} + \frac{1}{n_T}\sum_{i\in[T]}\big(y_i(1) - \overline{y(1)} - x_i'\beta_{I,T}\big) - \frac{1}{n_C}\sum_{i\in[C]}\big(y_i(0) - \overline{y(0)} - x_i'\beta_{I,C}\big) + o_p\Big(\sqrt{\frac1n}\Big).$$”
[The statement with the sequence made explicit] Consider a sequence of finite populations indexed by $n$ (dimension $d = d_n \le n$, covariates, potential outcomes and $n_T = n_{T,n}$ depending on $n$), under complete randomization at each $n$, satisfying Assumptions 1–3, with $\widehat L_T$ and $\widehat L_C$ invertible (footnote 4). If $\kappa_n \to 0$, then $$\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}_{I,\mathrm{Debiased}} - \big(\overline{y(1)} - \overline{y(0)}\big) - \frac{1}{n_T}\sum_{i\in[T]}\big(y_i(1) - \overline{y(1)} - x_i'\beta_{I,T}\big) + \frac{1}{n_C}\sum_{i\in[C]}\big(y_i(0) - \overline{y(0)} - x_i'\beta_{I,C}\big) = o_p\big(n^{-1/2}\big).$$ The proof shows more: without the condition $\kappa = o(1)$, the left-hand side is $O_p\big(\sqrt{\kappa/n}\big)$.

Opus followed B.4 and found the expansion correct with remainder $O_p(\sqrt{\kappa/n})$ under $\kappa = o(1)$; the proof as printed contains the swapped weight P005-E013 (P005-T10, P005-T11), the subscript slip P005-E012 (P005-T12, P005-T13), the missing transposes of P005-E010 and the wrong cross-reference P005-N007 (“the proof of Theorem 4.1” for the proof of Theorem 3.2), and it relies on the covariance variance bound of Lemma A.1 in its corrected form (P005-E002); the validator's derivation for P005-E002 (the artifact named, section 4) notes that the multiplier $\frac{n_C}{(n-2)n_T}$ has order $\frac1n$ under Assumption 3, so the repaired bound preserves the rate.
